metadata.title: An engagement-aware predictive model to evaluate problem-solving performance from the study of adult skills' (PIAAC 2012) process data

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses OECD PIAAC 2012 PS-TRE process-log data from three countries/economies (United States, South Korea, United Kingdom) and restricts analysis to a single PS-TRE booklet (PS1). The manuscript does not report the use of PIAAC sampling weights or any replicate-weight scheme (e.g., BRR/jackknife), nor does it name any weight variable (such as TOTWGT or W_FSTUWT). Because the models are deep-learning classifiers (LSTM with attention) trained on sequential process features, the authors appear to run an unweighted ML pipeline; however, the paper does not explicitly confirm this. For replication with the full PIAAC microdata, analysts should apply the official PIAAC complex-survey weights when estimating population-representative performance, and consider whether hierarchical clustering (students within units) is handled via weighting or design-based evaluation.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The dependent variables are engagement (binary) and task performance categories derived from PS-TRE process-log modeling, not PV-based cognitive achievement scores. As a result, plausible values are not part of the outcome construction in this study. The manuscript also does not describe any explicit missing-data strategy for the process-log sequences or derived engagement labels, which is a reporting gap because sequence models typically require rules for incomplete sequences, missing timestamps, or truncated logs.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The analysis uses the first round of the OECD PIAAC Main Study (2011–2012) and focuses on the cognitive domain of PS-TRE. The study restricts the dataset to the PS-TRE booklet PS1 and analyzes only the three countries/economies for which PS1 log data are available in the study (United States, South Korea, United Kingdom). The dependent engagement label is created using the T-disengagement method (Goldhammer et al., 2016; OECD, 2019) based on item-specific response-time thresholds, producing a binary engagement indicator per examinee-task. The paper does not report additional exclusions (e.g., minimum sequence length, missing timestamps) in the provided text.

main_findings.dataset_used: PIAAC 2012 PS-TRE (Booklet PS1) — adult sequential problem-solving process data (United States, South Korea, United Kingdom)
main_findings.target_variable: Problem-solving performance (categorical score) — predicted from process sequences
main_findings.performance_metrics: Best model: Effort-Aware Attention-LSTM. Overall (Table 2): United States ACC 0.802 (0.113), AUC 0.821 (0.110), F1 0.875 (0.106); South Korea ACC 0.859 (0.115), AUC 0.824 (0.120), F1 0.886 (0.108); United Kingdom ACC 0.883 (0.103), AUC 0.835 (0.098), F1 0.900 (0.097). Compared with Attention-LSTM: overall F1 ~0.82–0.83, ROC ~0.70–0.75, accuracy ~0.75–0.78.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PIAAC 2012 PS-TRE (Booklet PS1) process-log data from the United States, South Korea, and the United Kingdom, the study leveraged task engagement and directed-graph network statistics (centralization, density, flow hierarchy, shortest path, and related structure) to predict problem-solving performance categories, finding that the Effort-Aware Attention-LSTM improved performance across accuracy, ROC-AUC, and F1 relative to Attention-LSTM. This indicates that explicitly modeling examinee engagement alongside sequential process behavior can yield more accurate and potentially more valid interpretations of adult problem-solving performance in low-stakes digital assessment contexts, though the study is predictive and does not establish causal effects.

main_findings.dataset_used: PIAAC 2012 PS-TRE (Booklet PS1) — adult sequential problem-solving process data (United States, South Korea, United Kingdom)
main_findings.target_variable: Task engagement (binary engaged vs disengaged) — predicted from process sequences
main_findings.performance_metrics: Best model: Effort-Aware Attention-LSTM. Overall (Table 2): United States ACC 0.872 (0.050), AUC 0.878 (0.052), F1 0.937 (0.050); South Korea ACC 0.845 (0.017), AUC 0.857 (0.020), F1 0.881 (0.048); United Kingdom ACC 0.844 (0.082), AUC 0.858 (0.068), F1 0.920 (0.098). Task-level (Table 3): engagement F1 ranges roughly 0.892–0.998 with high accuracies; the paper reports the largest engagement-aware performance gains on Task 5 (F1 improved by +0.21 to +0.28; accuracy improved by +0.20 to +0.23).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PIAAC 2012 PS-TRE (Booklet PS1) process-log data from the United States, South Korea, and the United Kingdom, the study leveraged directed-graph network statistics derived from sequential actions to predict binary task engagement, finding that the engagement-aware Attention-LSTM achieved high engagement classification performance (overall F1 about 0.92–0.97 and ROC-AUC about 0.86–0.88). This indicates that engagement can be operationalized from interaction traces with strong predictive accuracy, supporting the use of engagement-aware scoring or validity checks in digital large-scale assessments, while causality cannot be inferred from the predictive modeling.

data.outcome_summary: The study analyzes OECD PIAAC 2012 PS-TRE process-log data (adult sequential problem-solving) restricted to booklet PS1 and three countries/economies (United States, South Korea, United Kingdom). It builds an effort-aware deep-learning framework that converts each examinee’s action sequence into a directed graph, summarizes it with network statistics, and feeds these representations into an LSTM with a global attention layer. Two model variants are compared: Attention-LSTM (performance only) versus Effort-Aware Attention-LSTM (performance and engagement jointly). Across countries, the effort-aware model improves performance prediction, with overall F1 rising from about 0.82–0.83 (Attention-LSTM) to about 0.88–0.90 (Effort-Aware), and engagement classification reaching F1 about 0.92–0.97. Evaluation uses threefold cross-validation with accuracy, F1, and ROC-AUC; however, the paper does not report a missing-data strategy and does not document whether PIAAC complex-survey weights were applied, limiting population-representativeness claims.
